# JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) Configuration

JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) comes with two configurations, *default* and
*profile*. These configurations are found under the `${JAVA_HOME}/lib/jfr`
directory. If no configuration is provided, the *default* configuration is used.
Please do not edit these files. Instead, create new ones.

JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) also provides an interactive tool for creating a
configuration that matches what you want to observe. You can enable everything,
but collecting more data increases JFR overhead.

**Reference**

- [JFR Configuration Improvements](https://inside.java/2022/06/13/sip055/)

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [JDK Mission Control (JMC)](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

## JDK Mission Control (JMC)

1. Download the latest version of JMC from
   [here](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html).

2. Specify the version of Java.

   When having multiple versions of Java installed, you may need to specify
   which one to be used by JMC. This can be done through the `jmc.ini` file,
   found under the `Eclipse` directory of where JMC is installed.

   Add the `-vm` option followed by the path to the `bin` directory, as shown
   next.

   ```
   ...
   -vm
   /Users/aattard/.sdkman/candidates/java/current/bin
   ...
   ```

   Please note that this file will contain other information, which is excluded
   for brevity.

## Build the application

The following examples require the application to be built.

```shell
./mvnw clean package
```

(*Optional*) Verify that the JAR file was created.

```shell
tree --sort=name './target/libs'
```

There should be one JAR file.

```
./target/libs
└── jfr-configuration-1.0.0.jar

1 directory, 1 file
```

Some of the following commands dump JFR files into a `jfr` directory. Make sure
that the `jfr` directory exists.

```shell
rm -rf './jfr'
mkdir -p './jfr'
```

## Use the *default* configuration


The *default* configuration provides a good balance between amount of
information collected and low overhead. The *default* configuration has an
overhead lower than 1% and is expected to be used in production. The *default*
configuration file can be found at `${JAVA_HOME}/lib/jfr/default.jfc`.

1. Run the application and use the *default* configuration.

   There are two ways to do this. Either:

   - Start the application without providing the configuration

     ```shell
     java \
       -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='Configuration',filename='./jfr/demo-default.jfr' \
       -jar './target/libs/jfr-configuration-1.0.0.jar'
     ```

      - Start the application by providing the *default* configuration
        (`settings=default`).

     ```shell
     java \
       -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='Configuration',filename='./jfr/demo-default-with-settings.jfr',settings=default \
       -jar './target/libs/jfr-configuration-1.0.0.jar'
     ```

   Note that you don’t have to provide the path to the configuration file, but
   just the configuration name (`default`) without the extension. JFR will know
   from where to pick up this file.

   The application will terminate automatically after 40 seconds.

   (*Optional*) Verify that the JFR file was created.

     ```shell
     tree --sort=name './jfr'
     ```

     The recording.

     ```
     ./jfr
     ├── demo-default.jfr
     └── demo-default-with-settings.jfr

     1 directory, 2 files
     ```

2. Print the recording summary.

   Filter the TLAB data.

   ```shell
   jfr summary './jfr/demo-default.jfr' | grep 'jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB' || echo 'No jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB events found'
   ```

   The *default* configuration does not collect TLAB data.

   ```
    jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB               0             0
   ```

3. (*Optional*) Open the flight recording file with JMC
   (`./jfr/demo-default.jfr`).

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-default.jfr"
   ```

## Use the *profile* configuration

The *profile* configuration provides more information than the *default*
configuration at the cost of higher overhead. JFR was designed to be as lean as
possible, and while the *profile* configuration adds to the overhead, this is
usually negligible. Do not hesitate to switch to this configuration when more
information is required. The *profile* configuration file can be found at
`${JAVA_HOME}/lib/jfr/profile.jfc`.

1. Run the application by providing the *profile* configuration
   (`settings=profile`).

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='Configuration',filename='./jfr/demo-profile.jfr',settings=profile \
     -jar './target/libs/jfr-configuration-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

   Note that you don’t have to provide the path to the configuration file, but
   just the configuration name (`profile`) without the extension. JFR will know
   from where to pick up this file.

   The application will terminate automatically after 40 seconds.

   (*Optional*) Verify that the JFR file was created.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The recording.

   ```
   ./jfr
   ├── demo-default.jfr
   ├── demo-default-with-settings.jfr
   └── demo-profile.jfr

   1 directory, 3 files
   ```

2. Print the recording summary.

   Filter the TLAB data.

   ```shell
   jfr summary './jfr/demo-profile.jfr' | grep 'jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB' || echo 'No jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB events found'
   ```

   The *profile* configuration does not collect TLAB data.

   ```
    jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB               0             0
   ```

3. (*Optional*) Open the flight recording file with JMC
   (`./jfr/demo-profile.jfr`).

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-profile.jfr"
   ```

## Create custom configuration

JFR provides an interactive command-line tool that helps create the right
configuration by asking a set of questions. The JFR configuration tool creates
a configuration based on the provided answers.

By default, JFR does not collect TLAB (Thread Local Allocation Buffer) data.
This provides insight into how the memory is being used by the application, such
as what objects are being created and from where. The following example shows
how we can capture TLAB events.

1. Create the custom configuration.

   ```shell
   jfr configure \
     jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB#enabled=true \
     jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB#enabled=true \
     jdk.PromoteObjectInNewPLAB#enabled=true \
     jdk.PromoteObjectOutsidePLAB#enabled=true \
     --output './jfr/custom.jfc'
   ```

   Alternatively, use the interactive option, as shown below, and follow the
   provided instructions.

   ```shell
   jfr configure --interactive --output './jfr/custom.jfc'
   ```

   Select option `4`, to collect the TLAB data, and accept the default for the
   rest.

   ```
   ============== .jfc Configuration Wizard ============
   This wizard will generate a JFR configuration file by
   asking 12 questions. Press ENTER to use the default
   value, or type Q to abort the wizard.

   Garbage Collector: Normal (default)
   1. Off
   2. Normal
   3. Detailed
   4. High, incl. TLABs/PLABs (may cause many events)
   5. All, incl. Heap Statistics (may cause long GCs)
   4
   Using: High, incl. TLABs/PLABs (may cause many events)
   ...
   ```

2. (*Optional*) A `.jfc` file will be created. This file can be saved anywhere
   on the filesystem as long as it is accessible. For this example, the `.jfc`
   is saved under the `jfr` directory.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The custom configuration.

   ```
   ./jfr
   ├── custom.jfc
   ├── demo-default.jfr
   ├── demo-default-with-settings.jfr
   └── demo-profile.jfr

   1 directory, 4 files
   ```

   The `.jfc` file is an XML file and can be viewed and edited manually.

3. Run the application by providing the path to the _custom_ configuration
   (`settings=./jfr/custom.jfc`). Note that here we had to provide the path to
   the configuration file and not just the name.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='Configuration',filename='./jfr/demo-custom.jfr',settings='./jfr/custom.jfc' \
     -jar './target/libs/jfr-configuration-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

4. Print the recording summary.

   Filter the TLAB data.

   ```shell
   jfr summary './jfr/demo-custom.jfr' | grep 'jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB'
   ```

   The custom configuration collects TLAB information.

   ```
    jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB               2            32
   ```

5. (*Optional*) Open the flight recording file with JMC
   (`./jfr/demo-custom.jfr`).

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-custom.jfr"
   ```

## Enable (and/or disable) events from command line

JFR events can be enabled or disabled from the command line without having to
create new configurations. This can be done by including the event canonical
name followed by `#enabled=true` to enable the event or `#enabled=false` to
disable it.

For example, to capture the `jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB` events, we can use
the default configuration and enable the event from the command line.

1. Run the application with the `jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB` events enabled
   (`jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB#enabled=true`)

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='Configuration',filename='./jfr/demo-command-line.jfr',jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB#enabled=true \
     -jar './target/libs/jfr-configuration-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

   Please note that earlier we enabled four events, while here we are enabling
   just one to keep the command as simple as possible. You can enable all four
   events by using the following (longer) command.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='Configuration',filename='./jfr/demo-command-line.jfr',jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB#enabled=true,jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB#enabled=true,jdk.PromoteObjectInNewPLAB#enabled=true,jdk.PromoteObjectOutsidePLAB#enabled=true \
     -jar './target/libs/jfr-configuration-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

2. Print the recording summary.

   Filter the TLAB data.

   ```shell
   jfr summary './jfr/demo-command-line.jfr' | grep 'jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB'
   ```

   The command-line configuration collects TLAB information.

   ```
    jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB               2            32
   ```

3. (*Optional*) Open the flight recording file with JMC
   (`./jfr/demo-command-line.jfr`).

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-command-line.jfr"
   ```
